name: St Erth station
text: St Erth station, at one end of this stretch, is listed Grade II and is the junction for the St Ives Bay Line.

name: Carnon Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Carnon Viaduct, 96 feet high, over Restronguet Creek. The first viaduct here had timber on stone piers; a new stone viaduct replaced it in 1933.

name: Ponsanooth Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Ponsanooth Viaduct over the River Kennal. At 139 feet high, it is the tallest viaduct west of Truro.

name: Collegewood Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Collegewood Viaduct, 954 feet long. When it was rebuilt in stone in 1934, it was the last timber viaduct in Cornwall to be replaced; the piers of the old one still stand.

name: Penmere station
text: Penmere station, at one end of this stretch, was opened by the Great Western Railway on July 1st 1925. Sidings to an oil depot there were in use from 1940 to 1967.

name: Pendennis Castle
text: Your train passes near Pendennis Castle, on the train's {side}, an artillery fort built for Henry VIII between 1540 and 1542. In the Civil War its Royalist garrison held out through a long siege until August 1646.

name: Treffry Viaduct
text: Your train passes beneath the Treffry Viaduct, built of granite by Joseph Treffry between 1839 and 1842 to carry his tramway, and water for his Fowey Consols mine, across the Luxulyan Valley.

name: Luxulyan
text: Your train passes near Luxulyan, on the train's {side}, which gives its name to luxulyanite, a rare Cornish granite used for the Duke of Wellington's sarcophagus in St Paul's Cathedral.

name: Holy well north-west of Roche station
text: Your train passes near an old holy well north-west of Roche station, on the train's {side}, protected as a scheduled monument.

name: Goss Moor
text: Your train crosses Goss Moor, a national nature reserve and the largest continuous mire in south-west Britain. The A30 once ran through the middle of it.

name: St Columb Road station
text: St Columb Road station, at one end of this stretch, was first called Halloon; it took its present name in 1878. It is a request stop.

name: Trenance Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Trenance Viaduct, 141 metres long, over the Trenance valley in Newquay. The first, of timber on stone piers, opened in 1849; today's masonry viaduct dates from 1939.

name: Liskeard Viaduct
text: Your train passes beneath Liskeard Viaduct, 150 feet high, which carries the main line. The Looe branch has run under it since 1901.

name: Coombe Junction Halt
text: At Coombe Junction Halt, at one end of this stretch, trains between Liskeard and Looe change direction: the driver and guard swap ends.

name: St Keyne Wishing Well Halt
text: St Keyne Wishing Well Halt, at one end of this stretch, shares its name with St Keyne's holy well. In Victorian times it was said that whichever of a newly married couple drank from it first would have the upper hand.

name: Liskeard and Looe Union Canal
text: Your train runs along the valley of the East Looe River, beside the remains of the Liskeard and Looe Union Canal. It was finished in 1828 with 24 locks, and fell out of use after the railway was built in 1860.

name: Old Guildhall, Looe
text: Your train passes near the Old Guildhall in East Looe, on the train's {side}, believed to date from around 1450.

name: Lelant Saltings
text: Your train runs beside Lelant Saltings, on the train's {side}, part of the Hayle Estuary, where the RSPB manages a nature reserve.

name: St Uny's Church, Lelant
text: Your train passes Lelant's parish church of St Uny, on the train's {side}, listed Grade I, with Norman work in its nave arcades.

name: Barbara Hepworth Museum
text: Your train passes near Trewyn Studio, on the train's {side}, which the sculptor Barbara Hepworth bought in 1949. She lived and worked there until her death in 1975; it is now a museum and sculpture garden.

name: Morwellham Quay
text: Your train passes near Morwellham Quay, on the train's {side} across the Tamar in Devon, a river port that grew up to serve the local mines. It is now an open-air museum.

name: Calstock Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the Tamar between Devon and Cornwall on Calstock Viaduct, 120 feet high, with 12 arches built from 11,148 concrete blocks between 1904 and 1907.

name: St Andrew's Church, Bere Ferrers
text: Your train passes near St Andrew's Church in Bere Ferrers, on the train's {side}, whose stained glass is the oldest in Devon outside Exeter Cathedral.

name: Tavy Bridge
text: Your train crosses the mouth of the River Tavy, just before it joins the Tamar, on the Tavy Bridge, 453 metres long.

name: St Budeaux connection
text: Your train uses a link between the two railways at St Budeaux, put in on March 21st 1941 so that trains could get round bomb damage. Since 1964, when the old line into Devonport closed, all trains from Victoria Road have used it.

name: Forde House
text: Your train passes near Forde House, on the train's {side}, enlarged around 1610. Charles I stayed there in 1625, and William of Orange in 1688, a few days after landing at Brixham.

name: Torre Abbey
text: Your train passes near Torre Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1196 for Premonstratensian canons and now the best-preserved medieval monastery in Devon and Cornwall.

name: Oldway Mansion
text: Your train passes near Oldway Mansion, on the train's {side}, built for the sewing-machine maker Isaac Singer and rebuilt by his son Paris in the style of the Palace of Versailles.

name: Cowley Bridge
text: Your train passes near Cowley Bridge, on the train's {side}, a three-arched classical bridge built in 1813 and 1814 by James Green, surveyor to the county of Devon.

name: Church of St Cyriac and St Julitta, Newton St Cyres
text: Your train passes near the parish church of Newton St Cyres, on the train's {side}, built in the 15th century of a reddish local volcanic stone. Inside is a standing effigy of John Northcote, who died in 1632.

name: Church of the Holy Cross, Crediton
text: Your train passes near Crediton's Church of the Holy Cross, on the train's {side}, on the site of the cathedral of the bishops of Crediton until the see moved to Exeter in 1050.

name: Roman forts at North Tawton
text: Your train passes near the site of Roman forts at North Tawton, on the train's {side}, where the Romans crossed the River Taw. The fort is thought to have been called Nemetostatio.

name: Okehampton Castle
text: Your train passes near Okehampton Castle, on the train's {side}, built between 1068 and 1086 after a revolt in Devon against Norman rule. It is now a ruin.

name: Copplestone Cross
text: Your train passes Copplestone Cross, on the train's {side}, an ancient carved granite pillar listed Grade I, standing where three old parishes meet.

name: Morchard Road station
text: Morchard Road station, at one end of this stretch, opened with the North Devon Railway on August 1st 1854.

name: Roman fort at Bury Barton
text: Your train passes near the site of a Roman fort at Bury Barton, on the train's {side}, thought to be a large early fort that was followed by a smaller one.

name: Church of St Thomas of Canterbury, Lapford
text: Your train passes near Lapford's church of St Thomas of Canterbury, on the train's {side}, listed Grade I. Inside is a late 15th-century screen, carved on both sides.

name: Gatehouse at Colleton
text: Your train passes near the gatehouse at Colleton, on the train's {side}, probably from the 1400s and listed Grade I. Its upper floor was once a chapel, licensed in 1402.

name: Kings Nympton station
text: Kings Nympton station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1854 as South Molton Road. It was renamed in 1951 to avoid confusion with South Molton station on the line to Taunton.

name: Portsmouth Arms station
text: Portsmouth Arms station, at one end of this stretch, is far from any village, so it is named after the nearby pub, itself named after the Earl of Portsmouth.
